title: Free 3 times a week full body hypertrophy program
summary: Answering a subscriber, NH lays out a 3-day full-body barbell-based hypertrophy program for novices/intermediates: each day opens with a 3x5 on a main lift, then 4x8 and 4x12 variations supersetted with pull-ups, arm work and light posterior-chain/face-pull work, finishing with abs, calves and neck. He then lists its limits: not for strength-focused or advanced lifters, little overhead press, not enough arm volume, and not for pure novices.

claims.claim: NH is not a big fan of full-body training, but it is more convenient and time-efficient than a split for people who can't get to the gym often.
Full body is best suited to novices and intermediates and may not be optimal for hypertrophy of certain muscles, though it still works.
NH is biased towards barbell movements; the program uses no machines and keeps isolation work light.

Monday: squat (high bar, low bar or front) 3x5; rack pulls below the knee or block pulls 4x8 superset pull-ups; close-grip bench 4x12 superset curls; light stiff-legged Romanian deadlift 15-20 reps superset face pulls; then abs, calves and neck.

Wednesday: flat bench 3x5 (weighted push-ups or weighted dips acceptable); deadlift variation (deficit, paused, snatch-grip, stiff-leg or RDL) 4x8 superset pull-ups; front squat, safety-bar squat or goblet squat 4x8 superset wrist curls; light hyperextensions 12-20 reps superset face pulls; then abs, calves and neck.

Friday: deadlift from the floor (conventional, sumo, trap bar or Jefferson) 3x5 (3x3 in the description); paused squats 4x8 superset pull-ups; dumbbell bench 4x12 superset skull crushers; overhead press (5x5 said in the video, 3x5 in the description) superset face pulls; then abs, calves and neck.
Treat a target of 8 reps as a 6-10 range: below 8 stay at the weight, above 8 add weight. The goal is to do 4x8 comfortably with good form before progressing.
A fixed number like 8 reps gives too little leeway to progress; thinking in a range solves this.
When adding weight NH puts 5 lb on each side of the bar; some prefer 2.5 lb per side depending on the lift.
For 4x12 close-grip bench: if all four sets of 12 are comfortable go up; if the last two sets only reach 10 and 9, stay at that weight.
Pull-ups in the supersets have no rep target (5 or 15 is fine) because they won't tax you; curls and skull crushers should stay at 8-12 reps or higher, never sets of 5.
Stiff-legged RDLs in this program must be light: the aim is to move through the range of motion and build the hamstrings, not to lift heavy.
Face pulls should be done for very high reps, on cable or bands.
Abs, calves and neck respond very well to frequency and volume; doing them every session, supersetted for about 15 minutes, gives good results without needing very heavy loads.
Dumbbell bench on Friday adds bench frequency while sparing the shoulders, since beginners easily develop overuse shoulder injuries if they flat bench too much.
Do skull crushers lying on a bench; standing versions are hard on elbows and wrists.
Opening each day with only 3x5 won't progress advanced lifters' main lifts; it is there to warm the body up and train a big compound lift while fresh without draining you like a 5x5 would.
For a bodybuilder, compound movements open the session but are not what drives hypertrophy; the subsequent movements, where most of the volume is accumulated, make you big.
The program is not for strength-focused lifters.
The overhead press is very important but taxing on lower back and shoulders for many, so it gets little focus in this novice-friendly program.
Pure novices shouldn't concern themselves with hypertrophy yet; NH believes everyone should first focus only on bench, squat and deadlift, then move to a structure like this once they have a base.
This program won't build big arms because there isn't enough biceps and triceps work, though novices and intermediates can still build a great physique with it.
